title: Europe Gas Storage at 14-Year Low as Winter Looms; Sinopec Ditches Middle East for Russian Crude; Libya Protests Shut Oil Fields
subhead: European gas storage sits at just 57% — the lowest August level since 2011 — while Sinopec scoops up 300,000+ bpd of Russian ESPO crude to dodge Hormuz disruptions, Libya's energy sector buckles under protests and blackouts, and Iran says its Oman-negotiated Hormuz shipping route is in 'final stages' but warns it won't guarantee security.

sections.heading: Europe Gas Storage at 2011 Lows as LNG Market Stays Squeezed
sections.body:
EU gas storage sites were only 57% full as of August 5, the lowest level for this time of year since 2011 and well below the nearly 70% full storage at the same point in 2025, according to Gas Infrastructure Europe data reported by OilPrice. The shortfall leaves Europe well behind its target of 80% storage by December and exposes the continent to severe price spikes if winter demand surges.

The root cause is the Iran war's disruption of Qatari LNG, which has flipped the global gas market into backwardation — near-term prices higher than future prices, discouraging the stockpiling Europe needs. Asia is outbidding Europe for available spot LNG, and Qatar — the world's top LNG exporter — has seen its shipments severely constrained by the Hormuz blockade.

Wood Mackenzie warned that European gas storage could end up below 70% ahead of winter 2026/27, with Massimo Di Odoardo, VP of Gas and LNG Research, noting: 'Low European inventories, strong Asian demand and limited new LNG supply growth almost guarantee elevated prices through this winter and into 2027.' David Lewis, senior research analyst at WoodMac, told Reuters that in a very cold winter, 'you might find that you have to do some sort of demand mitigation, higher prices, or else European markets would run out of gas.'
sections.whyItMatters: Europe is heading into winter with the thinnest gas cushion in 15 years. The Hormuz crisis isn't just about oil — it's gutting LNG supply too, and the backwardated market structure actively punishes storage. Without a major diplomatic breakthrough or a mild winter, Europe faces the real possibility of gas rationing.

sections.heading: Iran-Oman Hormuz Route in 'Final Stages' — But Security Not Guaranteed
sections.body:
Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Thursday that Iran and Oman have agreed on the 'geographical coordinates of the route' for commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, describing the deal as being in 'final stages of review and drafting,' the BBC reported. Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi told IRNA the new route would be temporary and could stay open for two to four months.

But Baghaei warned the agreement alone would not guarantee safe navigation, arguing security remained impacted by the US naval blockade of Iran's ports. The proposed deal reportedly gives Tehran control over ships entering the Gulf, according to Reuters — one of the biggest concessions yet to Iran. Iran is seeking transit fees of 5-7% of cargo value, while Oman has proposed around 3%, and Washington wants no fees at all.

President Trump claimed a broader deal could come 'as soon as Wednesday,' saying Iran would be 'hit very hard' if the strait did not open 'very soon.' US Secretary of State Rubio and Treasury Secretary Bessent both said talks had progressed, with Bessent telling CNBC a deal to reopen Hormuz could come 'today or tomorrow.' But Iran insists it is not negotiating with the US — only with Oman. And supreme leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has not appeared in public since the February strikes that killed his father, with President Pezeshkian acknowledging communication with Khamenei was 'difficult at the moment.'

Tanker traffic tells a different story from the diplomats. Only two vessels transited Hormuz on Wednesday, down from eight on Tuesday, according to Reuters. At Bab el-Mandeb, just one commodity vessel transited on Wednesday, down from 20 the day before, per Kpler data.
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between diplomatic optimism and maritime reality is as wide as ever. A 2-4 month temporary corridor with Iran controlling inbound traffic and charging transit fees is a major concession to Tehran — and markets are pricing in a reopening that shippers are not yet betting on. Two vessels through Hormuz on Wednesday is a near-complete shutdown, not a thaw.

sections.heading: Sinopec Pivots to Russian ESPO Crude as Middle East Supply Unravels
sections.body:
China's Sinopec, the world's largest refiner by capacity, has boosted purchases of Russian ESPO crude to 30-40 cargoes (241,000-320,000 bpd) for Q3 delivery, Reuters reported, citing trade sources and vessel-tracking data. The ESPO blend, loaded from Kozmino on Russia's Pacific coast, reaches China in about a week — far faster than West African or Brazilian alternatives — and comes at a discount.

The pivot reflects a structural shift. Chinese state-controlled refiners had suspended Russian crude purchases in October 2025 when the US sanctioned Rosneft and Lukoil, but resumed in March 2026 after Washington waived sanctions on Russian crude as the Iran war trapped Middle Eastern supply. Sinopec is not taking chances on Gulf supply: the certainty, price, and speed of Russian ESPO are now decisive factors.

Emma Li, lead China analyst at Vortexa, told Reuters: 'Rather than broad-based import growth, demand is shifting towards barrels with greater delivery certainty and lower freight costs — primarily onshore inventories and short-haul Russian Far East cargoes.' China has also eased fuel export curbs for a second consecutive month in August, allowing 2.7 million metric tons of product exports — a signal that Beijing now assesses domestic supply as secure enough to sell abroad, capitalizing on record global refining margins.
sections.whyItMatters: The US waiver on Russian crude sanctions, originally a wartime expedient, is reshaping trade flows in ways that will outlast the conflict. China's largest refiner is now structurally dependent on Russian ESPO — a pipeline that gives Moscow both revenue and leverage. When the war ends, reversing this dependency will be politically and logistically difficult.

sections.heading: Libya Protests Force Oil Field Shutdowns as Grid Collapses
sections.body:
Libya's energy sector is buckling under a compound crisis of blackouts, protests, and production shutdowns. Demonstrators stormed the Mellitah oil and gas complex, forcing the National Oil Corporation to halt operations at the El Feel oilfield and partially suspend the Wafa field, according to Al Jazeera. The gas supply disruption knocked out multiple electricity generation units, compounding outages that have left Libyans enduring 10-hour daily blackouts during a heatwave with temperatures exceeding 48 degrees Celsius (118F).

The protests, led by the Souq Al-Jumaa Movement and joined by activists in Tajoura and Janzour, targeted the Government of National Unity over corruption and service failures. Demonstrators shut down major roads, burned tires, and blockaded public buildings including the Foreign Ministry. A former official at GECOL, Libya's state electricity company, told Al Jazeera that major power projects launched before 2011 remain unfinished: the West Tripoli steam power station and the Gulf station near Sirte, both designed for 1,400 MW each, are years behind. Only two of Sirte's four units are connected to the grid.

The electricity crisis cascaded into a 400-kilovolt transmission line failure under peak summer demand, triggering cascading shutdowns at power stations and a sharp fall in grid frequency that led to a widespread collapse, according to Rabie Khalifa, spokesperson for Libya's eastern-based Ministry of Electricity. Egypt's resumption of electricity exports provided only about 70 MW — a fraction of Libya's needs.
sections.whyItMatters: Libya's energy sector is trapped in a feedback loop: political fragmentation prevents infrastructure investment, infrastructure failure triggers protests, protests shut down the oil and gas that funds the state, and production losses worsen the electricity crisis. With output already below pre-war levels and the Mellitah complex forced offline, Libya is a reminder that energy collapse can happen even in oil-rich states.

sections.heading: US Diesel Exports Hit Record as Domestic Stocks Slide to 1996 Lows
sections.body:
US diesel exports hit an all-time high of 1.9 million barrels per day last week, according to EIA data reported by OilPrice, breaking the previous record set in spring. Most of the exports are heading to Europe, where fuel supply is especially tight due to refinery closures and the Middle East disruption. But the export surge comes at a cost: US diesel inventories are now 12% below the five-year average, and at their lowest since 1996, Bloomberg reported.

The math is brutal. Refineries cannot produce more diesel at current run rates, and maintenance season begins in August, which will further tighten supply. Heating oil demand — also diesel-derived — will compound the squeeze as winter approaches. With domestic stocks already thin, the US is effectively subsidizing European fuel security at the expense of its own cushion.

The broader context: Phillips 66 reported Q2 earnings of $3.85 billion (up from $207 million in Q1), with realized refining margins jumping from $10.11 to $24.08 per barrel. Marathon Petroleum posted $8.5 billion in adjusted EBITDA. The geographic arbitrage created by the Hormuz disruption is generating windfall profits for refiners with access to non-Gulf crude — while draining inventories in the very countries supplying the exports.
sections.whyItMatters: The US is running down its own diesel reserves to supply Europe and capitalize on record margins. With heating season approaching and refinery maintenance about to cut supply, this is a bet that the Hormuz crisis eases before winter. If it doesn't, diesel shortages could become a domestic political problem.

sections.heading: UAE and Nigeria Fill the Gulf Vacuum — From Opposite Directions
sections.body:
The UAE has managed to boost oil exports to pre-crisis levels by June, becoming the Gulf producer with the most crude exiting Hormuz, Bloomberg reported. The UAE's strategy combines shuttling crude through the chokepoint onto larger vessels outside the Strait, maximizing its onshore pipeline from west to east, and shipping tankers through in dark mode. ADNOC issued its seventh crude tender since June, offering cargoes from ports inside and outside the Gulf, including ship-to-ship transfers offshore Fujairah and Malaysia. The UAE produced an estimated 4.1 million bpd in June — an all-time high — after leaving OPEC on May 1.

Nigeria, meanwhile, is emerging as the biggest West African beneficiary of the Hormuz disruption. Crude output hit 1.56 million bpd in June, the highest since April 2020, and 1.8 million bpd in July (including condensates). The NUPRC expects production to reach 2 million bpd 'in the near term.' Nigeria is pursuing $30-50 billion in investment across 22 offshore oil and gas projects over the next five years. And Angola's Sonangol and ANPG confirmed a successful appraisal well at Katambi-2 in Block 24, with initial flow tests showing 1,160 bpd of condensate and 41 MMscfd of gas — with potential to exceed 100 MMscfd.

India's refiners are the buyers snapping up this non-Gulf crude. HPCL and other Indian refiners have continued their West Africa crude buying spree, according to OilPrice, securing Nigerian and Angolan cargoes to replace Middle Eastern supply that can't reach them through Hormuz.
sections.whyItMatters: The Hormuz crisis is accelerating a structural rebalancing of global crude flows. The UAE is monetizing its OPEC exit at record output, Nigeria is pushing toward 2 million bpd, and Angola is developing new offshore reserves — all positioning themselves as Hormuz-free alternatives. India's pivot to West African crude may persist even after the strait reopens, reshaping trade routes that were stable for decades.

sections.heading: Aramco Deepens Asia Discounts as Gulf Export Routes Stay Squeezed
sections.body:
Saudi Aramco cut the September official selling price for Arab Light crude to Asian buyers by 50 cents per barrel, putting it at a $2 discount to the regional benchmark, OilPrice reported. The cut comes as Brent has dropped to around $80 per barrel — down roughly 20% in two weeks — on hopes that the Oman-Iran Hormuz deal will allow more tankers through the strait.

But Aramco's export reality remains constrained. CEO Amin Nasser said exports are near 5 million bpd, about 70% of normal volumes. The Kingdom has relied heavily on Yanbu on the Red Sea to keep crude moving, but Houthi threats at Bab el-Mandeb have made that route increasingly dangerous. The NCC WAFA tanker, hit by Houthi missiles off Yanbu roughly 1,000 km north of the declared blockade zone, demonstrated that rerouting north through the Red Sea is no longer safe. Dark-mode transits through Bab el-Mandeb have surged, with at least five tankers berthed at Yanbu on Saturday — the port's busiest day since the Houthi threat began.

Aramco has raised prices for some Medium and Heavy grades to Asia (mostly theoretical, since those barrels typically leave from the Persian Gulf), while cutting prices for all grades to the US, Northwest Europe, and the Mediterranean — a sign of competing for buyers who now have more supply options.
sections.whyItMatters: Aramco's price cut is a concession that Asian buyers have alternatives now — Russian ESPO, West African grades, and UAE tenders all compete for the same refiners. The 30% export reduction is the operational reality behind the diplomatic optimism about Hormuz. And with Houthi missiles reaching Yanbu, Saudi Arabia has no safe export route that doesn't involve either Hormuz or going dark.

bottomLine: August 7 brought the starkest illustration yet of the gap between diplomatic hope and physical reality. Iran says its Oman-negotiated Hormuz shipping corridor is in 'final stages' — but only two vessels transited the strait on Wednesday, and Iran's own deputy foreign minister says it would be temporary and give Tehran control of inbound traffic. Meanwhile, Europe's gas storage is at its lowest August level since 2011, US diesel inventories are at their lowest since 1996, and Libya's energy sector is in a feedback loop of blackouts, protests, and production shutdowns. Sinopec's pivot to 300,000+ bpd of Russian ESPO crude is the clearest signal yet that the Hormuz crisis is reshaping trade flows in ways that will outlast any temporary corridor deal. The UAE is producing at record highs, Nigeria is pushing toward 2 million bpd, and Aramco is cutting prices to keep Asian buyers — all signs of a global rebalancing that is happening faster than the diplomacy.
sources: BBC, OilPrice, Reuters, Bloomberg, Kpler, Windward, Gas Infrastructure Europe, Wood Mackenzie, EIA, Al Jazeera, IRNA, Anadolu Agency, NUPRC Nigeria, ANPG/Sonangol Angola, IEA, CNBC, Al Bawaba
